pages.title: Learn Xecute
pages.description: A guided path from your first Rust API to modules, testing, and integrations.

pages.title: Build your first API
pages.description: Install Xecute, run an API, and understand your first successful and invalid requests.

pages.title: Your first feature
pages.description: Generate a user feature, find the right files, change a rule, and run tests.

pages.title: How a request works
pages.description: Understand DTOs, controllers, services, repositories, and module imports.

pages.title: Features and setup
pages.description: Choose runtime features and understand what the generator configures for you.

pages.title: Upgrade an existing application
pages.description: Enable the five new runtime capabilities without assuming files are regenerated.

pages.title: Coming from NestJS
pages.description: Map NestJS concepts to the APIs actually implemented in Xecute.

pages.title: CLI reference
pages.description: Project creation, resource generators and supported flags.
pages.heading: CLI reference
pages.intro: Use this page when you know what you want to generate and need the exact command or flag. Run resource generators beside your application’s Cargo.toml.

pages.title: Development runner
pages.description: Watch, rebuild, recover from errors and shut down development processes.
pages.heading: Development server and hot reload
pages.intro: Keep a development server running while you edit Rust files. Start with a generated application; this runner rebuilds and restarts it when watched files change.

pages.title: Cargo workspaces
pages.description: Generate multiple applications with shared dependencies and tooling.
pages.heading: Multiple applications with Cargo workspaces
pages.intro: Choose a workspace when several applications should share dependency declarations and repository tooling. A single application does not need this setup.

pages.title: Update and uninstall
pages.description: Manage CLI installation without rewriting application source.
pages.heading: Update and uninstall
pages.intro: Update the installed CLI executable or remove it. Updating the CLI does not rewrite an application you already generated.

pages.title: Project structure
pages.description: Understand generated modules, server infrastructure and feature folders.
pages.heading: Project structure
pages.intro: Use this directory map to find the file you need to edit. Start in src/modules for feature work; use src/server for shared HTTP behavior.

pages.title: MVC and CQRS
pages.description: Choose service-based MVC or direct-handler CQRS generation.
pages.heading: MVC and CQRS
pages.intro: MVC uses a service to coordinate operations. CQRS gives each read or write its own handler. Both use DTOs and repositories; start with MVC if you are unsure.

pages.title: Providers and modules
pages.description: Register providers and enforce imports, exports and dependency boundaries.
pages.heading: Dependency injection and modules
pages.intro: Learn how Xecute creates dependencies and shares them between features. First understand the controller → service → repository flow; then read registration, imports, and exports below.

pages.title: Feature folders
pages.description: Keep DTOs, entities, repositories and tests together by feature.
pages.heading: Feature module folders
pages.intro: Keep one feature’s request types, records, storage, and tests together. Use this guide when your feature starts growing beyond its controller.

pages.title: Provider scopes
pages.description: Use singleton, transient and request lifetimes safely.
pages.heading: Provider lifecycles and HTTP requests
pages.intro: Choose how long an injected provider lives. Start with the generated singleton behavior; use request or transient scopes only when your application needs a different lifetime.

pages.title: Async startup and shutdown
pages.description: Initialize resources in dependency order and clean up after draining.
pages.heading: Async providers and application lifecycle
pages.intro: Use lifecycle hooks when resources must connect before requests start and close after work drains. Follow the async startup path below; attribute markers alone do not execute hooks.

pages.title: Controllers and extractors
pages.description: Route handlers, JSON bodies, path parameters and query DTOs.
pages.heading: Controllers and routing
pages.intro: A controller connects an HTTP request to an application operation. Use the example below inside a generated user feature, then choose body, path, or query inputs from the extractor table.

pages.title: DTO validation
pages.description: Reject malformed and invalid requests before application work.
pages.heading: DTO validation and errors
pages.intro: Put request rules in DTO structs under dto/mod.rs. Read the example, then use the status table to understand which requests are rejected before your handler runs.

pages.title: Middleware
pages.description: Compose app, controller and route middleware in documented order.
pages.heading: Middleware
pages.intro: Middleware wraps requests and responses around a handler. Use it for shared HTTP behavior; follow the execution order below before combining application, controller, and route middleware.

pages.title: Swagger and OpenAPI
pages.description: Generate OpenAPI schemas and serve local Swagger documentation.
pages.heading: Swagger and OpenAPI
pages.intro: Use Swagger to try endpoints and OpenAPI to describe their contract. Start with the generated /docs/ endpoint, then add metadata when you add routes or change DTOs.

pages.title: Errors and domain mappings
pages.description: Map failures to safe correlated HTTP error envelopes.
pages.heading: Exception handling and domain mappings
pages.intro: Turn application failures into safe HTTP responses. Choose a status and public message deliberately; keep internal errors out of the response.

pages.title: API version groups
pages.description: Mount explicit versioned routes and separate API documents.
pages.heading: API version groups and separate OpenAPI documents
pages.intro: Use explicit version groups when clients need different API contracts at the same time. Each group can have its own routes and API document.

pages.title: Multipart uploads
pages.description: Validate streaming uploads and use private local or optional S3 storage.
pages.heading: Multipart file uploads
pages.intro: Use this guide for multipart file requests. It needs the upload feature and explicit storage configuration; ordinary JSON endpoints do not need it.

pages.title: Static files
pages.description: Serve explicitly public assets without exposing application files.
pages.heading: Static files
pages.intro: Serve files that are intentionally public. Start with the generated public directory and /static/ prefix, then review path and fallback behavior before changing them.

pages.title: Application configuration
pages.description: Configure generated servers through validated TOML and environment secrets.
pages.heading: Application configuration
pages.intro: Start here to change generated server settings. Edit config/AppConfig.toml for application settings and use environment variables for secrets.

pages.title: Typed configuration
pages.description: Read reusable typed configuration with redacted validation errors.
pages.heading: Typed configuration
pages.intro: Use typed configuration when your own feature needs validated settings. Define a Rust type and read it at startup rather than parsing environment values inside every handler.

pages.title: Logging and exporters
pages.description: Configure structured logs, file rotation and custom exporter layers.
pages.heading: File logging and external logging backends
pages.intro: Start with console logs, then configure file rotation or an exporter when you need them. This guide shows which logging behavior belongs to your generated application.

pages.title: Server defaults
pages.description: Understand request limits, health endpoints and graceful shutdown policies.
pages.heading: Server defaults
pages.intro: Understand the policies your generated server already applies, including limits and health endpoints. Review this page before changing middleware or deploying.

pages.title: Welcome and startup URLs
pages.description: Discover enabled documentation, static assets and route version groups.
pages.heading: Welcome route and startup URLs
pages.intro: Use the welcome response and startup output to find your application’s enabled URLs. Only configured routes and documents appear.

pages.title: PostgreSQL
pages.description: Configure lifecycle-managed pools, migrations, repositories and transactions.
pages.intro: Replace in-memory storage when records must survive a restart. You need a PostgreSQL server, a connection URL, and the postgres feature; follow configuration, provider registration, then repository examples.

pages.title: Guards and JWT authentication
pages.description: Protect routes with verified users and role/permission policies.
pages.intro: Protect selected routes using verified identities. Configure a trusted token verifier before adding role or permission checks; reading an Authorization header is not authentication.

pages.title: Jobs and scheduling
pages.description: Run bounded process-local workers with retries, receipts and interval schedules.
pages.intro: Move suitable work out of a request handler into bounded workers. These jobs run in the current process and are not durable across restart; choose that model before configuring retries.

pages.title: Memory and Redis caching
pages.description: Use explicit TTL caching with bounded memory or namespaced Redis.
pages.intro: Cache data that can be recomputed, with an explicit key and expiration. Start with memory caching; use Redis only when you need that backend and have a Redis service available.

pages.title: CQRS buses and events
pages.description: Register typed command/query handlers, event subscribers and shared pipelines.
pages.intro: Use typed buses when you want central command/query dispatch or event subscribers. Generated CQRS already works through direct handler injection; adding buses is a separate application choice.

pages.title: Quality checks
pages.description: Run runtime, generator and generated-application checks.
pages.heading: Testing and quality checks
pages.intro: Run these commands from the generated application root before shipping a change. The page distinguishes application checks from checks for contributors working on Xecute itself.

pages.title: Testing modules and HTTP
pages.description: Override providers and exercise real routers in isolated tests.
pages.heading: Testing modules and HTTP assertions
pages.intro: Test HTTP behavior through a real router and replace providers when a test needs controlled data. Start with the generated feature tests, then use overrides for external dependencies.

pages.title: Runnable examples
pages.description: Find feature flags, commands and external services for each example.

pages.title: Deployment
pages.description: Build, containerize and operate generated applications.
pages.heading: Deployment
pages.intro: Deploy a generated application after it builds and passes tests locally. Follow the release/container instructions and supply your own production configuration and secrets.

pages.title: Development and packages
pages.description: Work on the CLI, runtime and macro crates.
pages.heading: Development and packages
pages.intro: This page is for changing Xecute itself, rather than building an application with it. It explains the repository packages and contributor checks.

pages.title: Troubleshooting
pages.description: Resolve common generation and application startup issues.
pages.heading: Troubleshooting
pages.intro: Find the symptom closest to yours in the table below. Read the full command output first, and check whether you are in the generated application or the Xecute repository.

pages.title: Scope and limitations
pages.description: Separate implemented capabilities from application extensions.
pages.heading: Scope and limitations
pages.intro: Check this page before planning around a capability. It separates generated behavior from features you must implement or configure in your application.

pages.title: Cargo feature reference
pages.description: Choose the Cargo flags and setup required for each runtime capability.

pages.title: Release process
pages.description: Understand crate versions, tags and generated GitHub release notes.
pages.heading: Changelog and GitHub releases
pages.intro: This page is for maintainers publishing Xecute packages. Application users normally want the CLI update guide instead.

pages.title: Changelog
pages.description: Review changes across Xecute releases.
pages.intro: Review changes before updating an existing application. Updating the CLI does not rewrite generated application files.

pages.title: AI agent skills
pages.description: Download the Xecute skill and complete machine-readable documentation for your coding agent.
